summary: Mike Padlipsky offers two solutions to the problem, raised in RFC 487, of sending a file to someone without knowing their password. One adds a convention so the recipient pulls the file, the other adds a command. They avoid the objections to a daemon approach raised in RFC 501.

eli5.summary: How do you give someone a package if you do not know their key? Either they come and pick it up, or the sender uses a special delivery method.

subtitle: Two ways to send a file to someone without knowing their password.

tldr.problem: FTP could not easily send a file to a recipient without the sender knowing the recipient's password, and using a daemon process raised access control concerns.
tldr.mechanism: One solution lets the recipient pull the file instead of the sender pushing it. Another adds a POOL command that places incoming files in a safe directory where the recipient can retrieve them.
tldr.outcome: Either approach solves the problem with fewer complications than using a daemon, and both respect each system's existing access control mechanisms.

today: While the specific POOL command was not adopted into the FTP specification, the conceptual solutions—pull-based transfer and intermediate safe storage—influenced later designs. Modern secure file transfer often uses these patterns: users authenticate and retrieve files themselves, or files are placed in intermediate locations for collection.

sections.title: The Problem: Sending Without a Password
sections.content: Users sometimes need to send files to other network users without knowing their passwords. Simply pushing the file as the sender would require the sender to have the recipient's credentials, which is insecure. Using a daemon process to do the work on behalf of the sender would require an interpretive access control mechanism different from most systems' normal mechanisms, as RFC 501 had pointed out.
sections.eli5: You need to send someone a file, but you do not know their password. A daemon doing it for you seems messy.

sections.title: The Pull Solution
sections.content:
Instead of the sender pushing the file, the recipient pulls it using their own credentials. The sender gives file permissions on their end, and the recipient uses their own FTP client to retrieve it. This works if the recipient has an account on the sender's system or if the system allows free guest FTP access.

The downside is that the recipient must be logged in and able to initiate the transfer. If the recipient is not available or the system is scheduled downtime, the transfer cannot happen immediately.
sections.eli5: The person who wants the file logs in and gets it themselves, solving the password problem.

sections.title: The POOL Solution
sections.content:
A new FTP POOL command places incoming files in a special pool directory rather than directly into the recipient's directory, then notifies the recipient of its arrival. The recipient can then copy it into their own directory. This prevents unauthorized users from freeloading or overwriting existing files.

The syntax POOL id name specifies the recipient id and the file name. The pool directory handles uniqueness transparently, and the recipient receives a notification (optionally with the sender's identity) to pick up the file.
sections.eli5: Place the file in a safe shared area and tell the person it arrived. They copy it when they are ready.

references.text: Pogran, K. "Comments on the File Transfer Protocol" (RFC 501).
